summary: Psalm 29 begins by summoning heavenly or mighty beings to give Yahweh glory. The poem then moves through a storm-like display of Yahweh’s voice over waters, forests, mountains, wilderness, animals, and temple praise. It ends with Yahweh enthroned as king and giving strength and peace to his people.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how praise in Psalms can use creation imagery to portray God’s rule. In Book I, it places David-associated worship in a cosmic frame: the power that shakes the world is also the power that blesses the people.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David.” In Psalms, Davidic headings are ancient features of the received collection, but readers differ on whether each one means authorship, association, dedication, collection, or reception.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities as Scripture and prayer.
context.date: Psalms is an anthology formed over time; this chapter’s exact date is not established by the chapter.
context.setting: The poem names waters, Lebanon, Sirion, the wilderness of Kadesh, Yahweh’s temple, and the Flood, but it does not narrate one dated event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and praise, using repetition, parallel lines, and vivid creation imagery.

outline.heading: Call to give Yahweh glory
outline.note: The psalm opens by telling the sons of the mighty to ascribe glory and strength to Yahweh and to worship him.

outline.heading: The voice over waters
outline.note: Yahweh’s voice is heard over the waters as thunder, power, and majesty.

outline.heading: The voice among mountains and trees
outline.note: The voice breaks the cedars of Lebanon and makes Lebanon and Sirion move like young animals.

outline.heading: The voice in lightning and wilderness
outline.note: The voice strikes with lightning and shakes the wilderness of Kadesh.

outline.heading: The voice and the temple cry
outline.note: The voice affects animals and forests, while everything in Yahweh’s temple says, “Glory!”

outline.heading: King forever, giver of peace
outline.note: Yahweh is enthroned at the Flood, remains king forever, and gives strength and peace to his people.

keyVerses.text: Ascribe to Yahweh the glory due to his name. Worship Yahweh in holy array.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the psalm’s opening summons: Yahweh is to be honored and worshiped.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh’s voice is powerful. Yahweh’s voice is full of majesty.
keyVerses.why: This compact line names the quality that the following images display.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh’s voice makes the deer calve, and strips the forests bare. In his temple everything says, “Glory!”
keyVerses.why: The verse brings together the force of Yahweh’s voice in creation and the answering cry of worship.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.
keyVerses.why: The psalm ends by connecting cosmic kingship with blessing for Yahweh’s people.

themes: Strength and peace for the people

questions.question: Who are “you sons of the mighty”?
questions.answer: The chapter does not define the phrase. It addresses a group capable of being summoned to give Yahweh glory and strength. Readers differ on whether the phrase points to heavenly beings, powerful rulers, or another exalted audience; the psalm’s main point is that even the mighty must honor Yahweh.

questions.question: What does “Ascribe” mean here?
questions.answer: In this psalm, “Ascribe” is a command to acknowledge or give recognition to what belongs to Yahweh. Verses 1-2 repeat the word three times, making the opening sound like a formal summons to worship.

questions.question: Is this psalm describing an actual storm?
questions.answer: The poem uses storm language: waters, thunder, lightning, broken cedars, shaking wilderness, and stripped forests. It does not give a weather report or date an event. The imagery depicts Yahweh’s voice as powerful over creation.

questions.question: Why does the psalm repeat “Yahweh’s voice” so often?
questions.answer: The repetition makes the voice the center of the poem’s movement. Each new line shows that voice in another sphere: waters, trees, mountains, lightning, wilderness, animals, and forests. The repeated phrase builds a cumulative picture of authority.

questions.question: What are Lebanon and Sirion doing in the psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 5 names the cedars of Lebanon, and verse 6 says Lebanon and Sirion skip like powerful young animals. The poem personifies places in creation, portraying even mountains or regions as affected by Yahweh’s voice. Sirion is a name for Mount Hermon, helping identify the place pictured in the poem.

questions.question: Why does verse 9 mention deer calving and forests being stripped bare?
questions.answer: The verse places living creatures and forests under the same overwhelming voice. The text does not explain the mechanism or invite a scientific explanation. Its poetic point is that Yahweh’s voice reaches from animal life to the forest canopy, and the temple answers with “Glory!”

questions.question: What does “the Flood” refer to?
questions.answer: Verse 10 says Yahweh sat enthroned at the Flood and sits as King forever. The chapter itself does not retell the Flood story; it uses the image to speak about Yahweh’s rule over overwhelming waters. The cross-references point readers to other flood and water passages for comparison, but Psalm 29’s claim is focused on kingship.

questions.question: How does a psalm full of thunder end with peace?
questions.answer: The final verse turns from the display of Yahweh’s power to what Yahweh gives his people. The same Yahweh whose voice shakes creation gives strength and blesses his people with peace. The psalm does not erase the terror of the imagery; it places that power under the rule of a king who blesses.

glossary.def: A command to attribute or give recognition. In verses 1-2 it calls the addressed beings to acknowledge Yahweh’s glory and strength.
The phrase used in verse 2 for the manner of worship. The chapter does not define the expression, but it connects worship with holiness and ordered honor.
Large trees named in verse 5. The psalm uses them to show the force of Yahweh’s voice, which breaks even what appears strong.
A place name in verse 6, paired with Lebanon. The line pictures both as moving like a young, wild ox.
The overwhelming waters named in verse 10. The psalm uses it to portray Yahweh enthroned as king.
The blessing named in verse 11. It is the final word of the chapter’s movement from glory, thunder, and shaking to Yahweh’s care for his people.
